title: Bark Ranch Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Bark Ranch wells have a 240 ft median depth, with most producing 5-15 gpm in fractured mountain bedrock.
h1: What Wells Are Like in Bark Ranch, Colorado
intro_html:
Bark Ranch is a mountain well area where most permits serve domestic or household use. In records within 5 miles, the median well depth is 240 feet, and the middle half runs from 110 to 400 feet. Reported yields are generally usable: the median is 7.0 gallons per minute, with a middle half from 5.0 to 9.0 gallons per minute.

These records describe fractured mountain bedrock rather than a predictable shallow basin aquifer. A nearby well can help set expectations, but it does not guarantee the same depth or yield for a new lot. Before buying, review the permit history, construction details, static water levels, and the proposed septic and building layout.

sections.heading: Bark Ranch well depth reflects fractured mountain rock
sections.html:
Completed wells near Bark Ranch have a median reported depth of 240 feet. The middle half is between 110 and 400 feet, while the 90th percentile is 600 feet. The deepest well in the records reaches 1,428 feet.

The depth mix shows why a single neighboring well is not enough for a bid: 20% are under 100 feet, 36% are from 100 to 300 feet, 33% are from 300 to 600 feet, and 10% are 600 feet or deeper. Most permits name an unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifer. Granite and gneiss can produce water along fractures, so the driller is estimating where those fractures may occur rather than following a uniform water-bearing layer.

sections.heading: What a Bark Ranch well may produce
sections.html:
The reported median yield is 7.0 gallons per minute. The middle half of reported results is 5.0 to 9.0 gallons per minute, and 70% of reported wells fall between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. That is a reasonable production range for many household uses, but the result still depends on storage, fixtures, livestock, irrigation, and how the well is tested.

Low production is present but not dominant: 3% of reported yields are under 1 gallon per minute, 19% are from 1 to 5, and 8% exceed 15. Ask for the well test and pump setting, not just a verbal yield. A low-yield well may still work with a storage tank, while a strong test does not remove the need for water-quality testing.

sections.heading: Water levels in Bark Ranch deserve a closer look
sections.html:
Among the 57 wells reporting static water levels, the median depth to water is 48 feet. The middle half ranges from 15 to 100 feet below the surface. That spread matters for pump selection, trenching, and estimating how much standing water is available in the casing.

The decade figures show a notable change in the available records: the median measured water level was 30 feet below surface in the 2010s and 100 feet in the 2020s. This suggests lower measured water levels in the newer group, but it is not proof of a basin-wide decline. Only 57 records include a static level, and measurement conditions, well locations, and seasons may differ. Treat the trend as a reason to investigate, not as a guaranteed forecast.

sections.heading: Bark Ranch permit history and active drillers
sections.html:
Permit records within the study area include 1,460 wells, with 975 recorded as constructed. The records show the busiest permitting period in the 1970s, with 295 permits. There were 206 in the 1980s, 268 in the 1990s, 166 in the 2000s, 87 in the 2010s, and 60 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025.

The most active drillers named in the records are Ground Water Systems Inc (Wilson, Richard R.) with 295 wells, Ingram Drilling Inc. (Ingram, Stephen E.) with 185, and Norris & Sons (Norris, T A) with 76. That history can help you compare local construction patterns, but it is not an endorsement or a guarantee of availability.

sections.heading: What drilling a Bark Ranch well can cost
sections.html:
Bark Ranch drilling runs through fractured mountain bedrock, so the footage is the main variable. The stated drilling rate is $65 to $100 per foot. At the median depth of 240 feet, the drilled hole models to about $15,600 to $24,000.

A finished system costs more than the hole. Including the pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical work, the modeled total at that depth is about $21,600 to $36,000. A lot requiring a deeper hole can move well beyond that range; the recorded 90th-percentile depth is 600 feet. Get a written proposal that separates drilling, casing and grout, pump equipment, water testing, trenching, electrical work, permits, and any unsuccessful-hole terms.

sections.heading: Bark Ranch risks: water quality, dry holes, and site layout
sections.html:
Fractured-bedrock wells can vary sharply from lot to lot. The records show 3% of reported yields under 1 gallon per minute, and the depth range includes wells reaching 1,428 feet. A driller cannot promise a productive fracture. Confirm the contract language for a low-yield or dry hole before work starts, and keep money available for a deeper attempt or storage solution.

Environmental screening also matters. Within about 10 miles are 4 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 620 historic mine features, and 58 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Their presence does not prove a problem at a particular parcel, but it supports laboratory testing before occupying the home and periodic testing afterward. Locate the well, septic system, replacement area, driveway, and building envelope together. Septic setbacks, access for a rig, casing and grout, and electrical trenching can affect both feasibility and cost.

sections.heading: Before buying or building near Bark Ranch
sections.html:
Start with the Colorado Division of Water Resources permit and the construction report for the parcel and nearby wells. Look for actual depth, tested yield, static water level, casing, pump information, and permitted use. Domestic or household use accounts for 92% of the local permit mix, while stock is 2%, irrigation is 1%, and monitoring is 2%. A permit is not the same as a completed, producing well.

For a vacant lot, have a local driller review access and likely well location before closing. Confirm the legal water right and any augmentation requirement that may apply in an over-appropriated basin. For an existing home, order a flow test and independent water-quality testing. Compare nearby areas such as Hidden Lake, Jamestown, Gold Hill, Ward, Sunshine, and Lazy Acres only as local context; the parcel's own geology and permit history control the final answer.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Bark Ranch?
faq.a: The median reported well depth near Bark Ranch is 240 feet. The middle half runs from 110 to 400 feet, and the 90th percentile is 600 feet. About 20% are under 100 feet, while 10% are 600 feet or deeper. Because the area is fractured mountain bedrock, nearby wells can differ substantially.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Bark Ranch?
faq.a: The modeled drilling rate is $65 to $100 per foot. At the 240-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $15,600 to $24,000. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical work is estimated at $21,600 to $36,000. A deeper hole, difficult access, or a dry-hole attempt can change the final price.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Bark Ranch?
faq.a: The median reported yield is 7.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 5.0 to 9.0 gallons per minute. About 70% of reported wells produce between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. Low production is possible: 3% report under 1 gallon per minute. Request the actual well test and ask about storage if the yield is limited.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Bark Ranch?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from the permit record alone. Within about 10 miles are 4 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 620 historic mine features, and 58 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those locations do not prove contamination at a specific property. Test the existing well through an independent laboratory, and ask a qualified professional which contaminants fit the parcel's history.

faq.q: Are water levels dropping in Bark Ranch?
faq.a: The available records show a higher median measured depth to water in the 2020s: 100 feet below surface, compared with 30 feet in the 2010s. However, only 57 wells report static water levels, and measurements may differ by location, season, and method. The data justify checking recent neighboring wells, but they do not prove a uniform groundwater decline.
